title: Education The Next 30 Years (RP) Schooling Alone
author: The Next 30 Years
summary: Delivered as a commencement address to Atlanta Classical Academy's Class of 2026, this essay argues that AI-driven educational personalization poses a civic threat: as each student is taught differently and individually, the shared intellectual inheritance that enables citizens to communicate, cooperate, and live together erodes. The author draws a parallel to the shift from communal moviegoing to personalised streaming -- technically an improvement in choice, but a loss of shared cultural experience -- and applies this logic to education. The essay acknowledges that personalization can improve individual outcomes but insists that education has always served two functions: giving students a common vocabulary and a common world. Classical education, the author argues, is resistance to this trend: graduates who have read the same texts and wrestled with the same questions share something that mere individual excellence cannot replace. The central challenge posed to graduates is the question their generation must answer: If everyone is taught differently, what will you still share?
points: * Education has always done two things at once: giving students a common vocabulary (the ability to understand one another) and a common world (a shared experience of having wrestled with the same ideas together) -- and AI-driven personalization threatens both simultaneously. * The McGuffey Readers became nearly universal not through top-down mandate but because a common culture naturally reproduced itself through schools, churches, and families -- demonstrating that shared educational experience is a product of cultural coherence. * The shift from communal moviegoing to personalised streaming is the analogy for what is happening to education: we have more choice than ever, but fewer shared touchstones that allow us to speak in cultural shorthand with one another. * A society depends not just on well-informed individuals but on people who share enough in common to understand, communicate, and cooperate with one another -- and this social cohesion has historically been produced, in part, by shared educational experience. * Classical education -- reading what others have read for generations, wrestling with the same questions -- is a form of resistance to the individualisation of culture, carrying a shared inheritance that personalised AI tutoring structurally cannot provide.
quotes: For most of American history, education was understood, however imperfectly, not merely as a private good, but as a common civic experience. In different schools and across states, students encountered many of the same books, historical narratives, ideas, and cultural touchstones, creating at least some shared intellectual inheritance.
We have fewer shared experiences. Fewer things we can assume everyone knows. Fewer moments that bind us together in a common cultural life.
Education has always done two things at once: It gave us a common vocabulary and a common world. Your classical education means you have been given both.

A common world is something different. It means you've experienced something together. You've read the same books -- not just heard of them, but wrestled with them. You've struggled with the same questions and ideas, sat in the same classrooms, and been shaped -- at least in part -- by the same things.
A society depends not just on individuals who are well-informed, but on people who share enough in common to understand one another -- to communicate, to cooperate, to live together.

Now, for the first time, we have technology -- artificial intelligence -- that can actually deliver on that promise in ways no teacher possibly could. It can adjust explanations instantly. It can provide unlimited practice. It can meet each student exactly where they are. That sounds like progress because, in many ways, it is.
If everyone is taught differently, what will you still share?
